The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2022-03-30.229.1) to [pass the bill](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/) in the Senate. The bill will now be sent back to the House of Representatives where our MPs will consider whether they agree with Senate amendments. ### What does the bill do? According to the [bill homepage](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6833), the purpose of the bill is to: * *provide that specified critical infrastructure assets must adopt and maintain a critical infrastructure risk management program;* * *provide for annual reporting obligations for assets that are exempt from the risk management program obligation;* * *make minor amendments in relation to consultation requirements and immunities;* * *provide for additional cyber security obligations that may be applied in relation to systems of national significance;* * *provide that directions facilitating government assistance to industry in the event of a serious cyber security incident prevail over the requirements of a risk management program;* * *amend provisions that authorise the use and disclosure of protected information;* * *provide that the minister's power to privately declare an asset as a critical infrastructure asset includes a power to require compliance with a risk management program; and* * *enable the minister to declare a critical infrastructure asset to be a system of national of significance; and include additional reporting requirements.* See the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd055) for more detailed information.

The speaker argued that the government breached long-standing national security convention by debating the Security Legislation Amendment (Critical Infrastructure Protection) Bill 2022 before the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security could complete its inquiry, and moved an amendment stating the government had substituted bipartisan cooperation for political expediency.

The speaker argued that the Labor Party's second reading amendment to the Security Legislation Amendment (Critical Infrastructure Protection) Bill 2022 is overly broad, allowing debate on virtually any topic, and accused Labor of playing "stupid, undergraduate games" with the amendment.

The Security Legislation Amendment (Critical Infrastructure Protection) Bill 2022 requires critical infrastructure entities to maintain risk management programs and allows the declaration of nationally significant systems. The speaker cited 1,600 cyber incidents handled by the Australian Cyber Security Centre in two years, with 400 affecting critical infrastructure, and argued the bill is urgently needed to protect essential services.

The Morrison government is breaking a longstanding bipartisan convention by forcing a vote on the Security Legislation Amendment (Critical Infrastructure Protection) Bill 2022 before it has been reviewed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, and has repeatedly politicised and mismanaged national security and defence policy, including abolishing the dedicated cybersecurity minister role and bungling major defence procurements.

The government introduced the Security Legislation Amendment (Critical Infrastructure Protection) Bill 2022, requiring critical infrastructure entities to implement risk management programs and comply with enhanced cybersecurity obligations for systems of national significance, using a principles-based framework and industry collaboration through the Trusted Information Sharing Network (TISN).

The speaker presented four reports from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security: advisory reports on the Security Legislation Amendment (Critical Infrastructure Protection) Bill 2022 and the National Security Legislation Amendment (Comprehensive Review and Other Measures No. 1) Bill 2021; an inquiry into national security risks affecting the higher education and research sector; and a statement on the review of regulations listing Hizballah and The Base as terrorist organisations.

Four unanimous bipartisan reports were tabled covering Hezbollah and The Base listings, national security risks in higher education, the critical infrastructure protection bill, and national security legislation amendments. The speaker welcomed the government's decision to list the entirety of Hezbollah as a terrorist organisation and supported passing the critical infrastructure bill despite consultation concerns, while noting many Richardson review recommendations remain outstanding.

National Security Legislation Amendment (Comprehensive Review and Other Measures No. 1) Bill 2021 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

The government introduced the National Security Legislation Amendment (Comprehensive Review and Other Measures No. 1) Bill 2021, implementing 13 recommendations from the Richardson comprehensive review and the 2017 independent intelligence review. The bill includes emergency authorisation for intelligence agencies to assist Australians at imminent risk overseas, extends travel document suspension from 14 to 28 days, and requires agencies to publish privacy rules.

The speaker announced the National Security Legislation Amendment (Comprehensive Review and Other Measures No. 1) Bill 2021, which implements some recommendations from Dennis Richardson’s review of the national intelligence community and rejects one, while also adopting measures from the 2017 Independent Intelligence Review. The bill includes 14 schedules addressing operational challenges for ASIO, ASIS, ASD, AGO, DIO, and ONI, such as emergency authorisations for intelligence on Australians overseas, class-based ministerial authorisations for terrorist-linked persons, and expanded onshore ASIS support for ASIO, with the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security recommending passage subject to a clarification on lawyer protections.

The National Security Legislation Amendment (Comprehensive Review and Other Measures No. 1) Bill 2021 was presented, with the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security recommending it be passed without amendments. A replacement explanatory memorandum was also tabled, incorporating the committee's recommendation and additional text requested by the Senate Scrutiny of Bills Committee.

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 lowers the registration threshold for political campaigners from $500,000 to $100,000 in electoral expenditure, and introduces a new requirement to register if spending at least $14,500 and one-third of revenue. The bill implements recommendation 18 of the JSCEM report on the 2019 federal election to align transparency rules for political actors with those for parties and candidates.

Labor opposed the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021, arguing it would lower the political campaigner threshold for charities and not-for-profits from $500,000 or two-thirds of annual income to $100,000 or one-third, imposing heavy disclosure requirements and foreign-donation bans that silence critics. The speaker moved a second reading amendment calling for the donation disclosure threshold to be reduced from $14,500 to a fixed $1,000 with real-time disclosure, and criticised the Morrison government for failing to deliver a national anti-corruption commission and for pursuing voter ID laws.

The speaker argued the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 would enhance transparency by requiring organisations spending over $100,000 or $14,500 (if over a third of annual revenue) on electoral expenditure to register as political campaigners, implementing recommendation 18 of the 2019 election inquiry. The speaker also detailed personal experiences of abuse during the 2019 campaign in the marginal seat of Robertson, including a verbal tirade at Woy Woy pre-poll, and condemned such behaviour as undemocratic.

The bill extends donation disclosure requirements to all political campaigners, not just political parties, to reduce foreign interference and increase transparency in electoral funding. The reforms follow the 2019 election inquiry which heard about intimidation of candidates, including the member for Boothby.

The speaker supported the bill's original provisions lowering the registration threshold for political campaigners from $500,000 to $100,000, but opposed the government's last-minute addition of 35 new provisions without consultation, moving an amendment to postpone the vote and calling for a lower disclosure threshold of $1,000.

The bill reduces thresholds for registering as a political campaigner, imposing retrospective compliance costs on charities and small community groups, while the speaker argued it is a cynical attempt to protect the major-party duopoly rather than genuinely increase transparency.

The speaker argued that the government's Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 would silence charities and stifle democracy, contrasting it with Labor's proposed real-time disclosure of political donations with a $1,000 threshold. They noted the 'Hands Off Our Charities' coalition of 100 leading charities, including Anglicare Australia, Amnesty International, and the Australian Conservation Foundation, opposes the bill.

The bill lowers the threshold for registering as a political campaigner from $500,000 to $100,000 or one-third of annual income, which would burden small local advocacy groups like Save Willow Grove, Parramatta Park campaigners, and Westmead Push for Palliative Care with excessive red tape, while failing to address the need for broader transparency reforms through proper consultation.

The speaker argued that the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 targets smaller charities, environmental groups, and unions—such as the Australian Conservation Foundation, Bob Brown Foundation, WWF, RSPCA, St Vincent de Paul, and several unions—to silence dissent and protect the government, rather than improving transparency or democracy.

The speaker thanked committee members and commended the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 to the House, arguing it strengthens election integrity by extending funding disclosure requirements to political actors and modernising the Commonwealth Electoral Act to protect voters from being misled.

The speaker argued that the government's 35 last-minute amendments to the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021 would restrict freedom of speech and apply retrospectively, targeting charities and welfare groups while ignoring billionaires like Clive Palmer who buy elections. They opposed the amendments, calling the process a strategy to silence critics and pander to the far right, and demanded caps on corporate and billionaire donations instead.

The bill would change the military discipline system for the Australian Defence Force.
It would expand the disciplinary infringement scheme for minor breaches, remove one level of summary authority, and create new service offences.
The new offences include failure to perform duty, cyber-bullying, and failure to notify a change in circumstances affecting a benefit or allowance.
Expands the disciplinary infringement scheme to deal with minor breaches of military discipline more effectively.
Removes the subordinate summary authority to simplify the enforcement of minor disciplinary issues.
Introduces new service offences for failure to perform duty, cyber-bullying, and failure to notify a change in circumstances.
Members of the Australian Defence Force and those administering military discipline.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2021-12-01.184.8) to agree with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). This means they can now discuss it in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bill homepage](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6751), the bill was introduced to: * *expand the operation of the disciplinary infringement scheme to provide a means of dealing with minor breaches of military discipline;* * *remove the subordinate summary authority and correct a number of anomalies with regard to the respective jurisdiction of discipline officers and summary authorities, and between the different types of summary authority, in relation to the type of breach of military discipline, the rank of defence members with which each can deal, and the powers and punishments available to each level of authority; and* * *establish new service offences for failure to perform duty or carry out an activity, cyber-bullying, failure to comply with removal order (in relation to material on social media that constitutes cyber-bullying) and failure to comply with requirement to notify change in circumstances (in relation to the receipt of a benefit or allowance).* Read more about the bill in the parliamentary library's [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd033).

A cyberbullying offence will apply when a defence member has used a social media service or relevant electronic service in a way that a reasonable person would regard in all the circumstances as threatening, intimidating, harassing or humiliating another person.* ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 3, item 2, page 48 (line 2), omit "as offensive or", substitute "in all the circumstances".* ### What does the bill do? The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 was introduced to reform the military discipline system, including expanding the disciplinary infringement scheme with a new senior discipline officer role, removing the subordinate summary authority, and adding new service offences for cyberbullying, receipt of a benefit or allowance, and failure to perform a duty.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 introduces a three-tier disciplinary system to streamline minor breaches via infringement notices, reduce delays, and improve mental health outcomes for ADF personnel, while also addressing cyberbullying as a new offence.

The speaker cautiously welcomed the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021, which expands the disciplinary infringement scheme and introduces new offences including cyberbullying, but criticised insufficient consultation and announced Labor would refer the bill to a Senate committee inquiry, reserving final position until the inquiry reports.

The speaker expressed condolences for two soldiers who died near Townsville and supported the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021, arguing it would streamline handling of minor disciplinary matters while preserving members' rights. They also criticised the Prime Minister for using the Australian national flag as a face mask during COVID and backed referring the bill to a Senate committee for scrutiny by 14 October.

The speaker argued that the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 will provide commanders with better tools to manage disciplinary matters efficiently and fairly, introducing new service offences such as cyberbullying to maintain morale and operational capability in the ADF.

The speaker supported the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021, arguing it modernises the military justice system by introducing cyberbullying as a specific offence and improving efficiency for lower-level disciplinary processes. The speaker also paid tribute to ADF personnel involved in the Afghanistan withdrawal and the 41 fallen Australian service members.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 was argued to be necessary for modernising military discipline, enabling faster resolution of workplace issues and adapting to changing societal expectations and technology.

The speaker acknowledged the 70th anniversary of the ANZUS treaty and referenced recent events at Hamid Karzai International Airport while addressing the Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Discipline Reform) Bill 2021 was commended to the House, reforming military discipline under the Defence Force Discipline Act 1982 by allowing minor breaches to be managed as disciplinary infringements and introducing a new cyberbullying service offence for the Australian Defence Force.

The majority voted in favour of agreeing with the main idea of the bills - known as reading them [for a third time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/) - which means they are now passed in the Senate. Because they have already passed the House of Representatives, they will now become law. ### What do the bills do? According the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd018): > *The purpose of the Data Availability and Transparency Bill 2020 (the Bill) is to establish a new data sharing scheme (‘the scheme’) which will serve as a pathway and regulatory framework for sharing public sector data. The Bill also establishes a new independent regulator, the National Data Commissioner, to oversee this process, and an Advisory Committee to assist the Commissioner. The purpose of the Data Availability and Transparency (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2020 (the consequential Bill) is to make amendments to other existing Acts. These amendments are necessitated by provisions in the Bill.*

The Data Availability and Transparency (Consequential Amendments) Bill amends the ASIO Act, the ADJR Act, the Privacy Act and the FOI Act to support the principal data sharing scheme, including allowing ASIO to advise on accreditation, limiting foreign entities' notice and review rights, enabling complaint transfers between commissioners, and preserving FOI protections for shared data.

Labor moved an amendment to pass the Data Availability and Transparency Bill 2022 on conditions including appointing a Data Commissioner, abolishing the Digital Transformation Agency's staffing cap, limiting consecutive labour-hire contracts, and publishing the Digital Review. Labor supported the revised bill after securing changes that removed foreign and private sector access and strengthened privacy safeguards, citing failures like robodebt and risks from big-tech data exploitation.

The Data Availability and Transparency Bill is a belated response to the Productivity Commission’s 2017 inquiry, aiming to enable controlled public-sector data use for public interest purposes. The speaker noted potential benefits such as on-demand buses and individualised services, but warned of risks including algorithmic failures like robodebt, privacy breaches, and manipulation, and welcomed the removal of the original bill’s provisions extending the scheme to foreign organisations and the private sector.

The Data Availability and Transparency Bill establishes a new scheme for sharing Australian government data, with amendments to enhance privacy protections and introduce national security safeguards, including that the scheme will not initially extend to the private sector and that foreign entities cannot become accredited. The government supports committee recommendations for ongoing security oversight, consideration of national security risks in higher education, and strengthened privacy protections such as prohibiting re-identification of de-identified data and requiring consent for biometric data sharing.

The Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 was moved to establish a governance board for the APVMA, streamline chemical reporting processes, and introduce incentives for including priority uses on product labels. The bill creates a part-time board with a chair, CEO, and three members, extends data protection periods up to five years for certain uses, and broadens the APVMA's enforcement powers.

The speaker criticised the government for moving the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority from Canberra to Armidale, arguing it was politically motivated and caused staff losses, and noted the government later breached its own policy order by allowing up to 50 staff to work in Canberra. The opposition supported the bill's efficiency measures but condemned the government's repeated delays on agricultural legislation.

The speaker supported the bill to establish a governance board for the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority, improving oversight of chemicals like glyphosate, and noted agriculture employs 329,000 Australians, with a goal of becoming a $100 billion industry by 2030.

The speaker argued that the relocation of the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) from Canberra to Armidale was a destructive, anti-science move that cost hundreds of millions of dollars, caused the loss of half its scientific staff, and created major delays. The bill establishes a governance board costing $400,000–$600,000 annually, which industry groups oppose, and the speaker criticised the government for lacking transparency and prioritising votes over science.

The Agricultural and Veterinary Chemicals Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 establishes a five-person skills-based governance board for the APVMA, ceases the advisory board, and introduces measures to streamline processes, enable computerised decision-making, strengthen sanctions for misleading information, and improve voluntary recall transparency.
